changes.old: SBE Position Statement: Personal Technology Use in CT Schools (2024)
No statewide mandate (opt-in grant funds physical lockable pouches)

states.Details: Local boards of education must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ use and operation, or possession of a wireless communication device in any public elementary or secondary school building or grounds thereof during the instructional day, with specified exceptions.
School districts must adopt a policy on students’ possession and use of non-school-issued wireless telecommunications devices during regular school hours, with specified exceptions.
School district governing boards and charter school governing bodies must adopt a policy limiting students’ use of wireless communication devices during the school day, with specified exceptions.

Public school districts and open-enrollment public charter schools must adopt a policy restricting students’ possession and use of a personal electronic device during the school day and prohibiting students’ use of a personal electronic device during the school day, with specified exceptions.

School district governing bodies, county offices of education, and charter schools must adopt a policy limiting or prohibiting students' use of smartphones while at a school site or while under the supervision and control of an employee, with specified exceptions.
states.VerificationNote: AB 3216 (the Phone-Free Schools Act, signed Sept 2024, compliance deadline July 1, 2026) requires every district, county office of education, and charter school to adopt a policy limiting or prohibiting student smartphone use - but the law explicitly leaves the compliance METHOD to local school boards, ranging from Yondr-style pouches to simply requiring phones be off and zipped in a backpack. Because software solutions aren't precluded, this doesn't meet the bar for a hard physical-storage mandate. The keyword classifier previously misread this as Restricted, almost certainly because the actual bill text lists a locked pouch as one EXAMPLE compliant method rather than a requirement - exactly the 'optional, not mandatory' case the classifier's negation/optionality scan is meant to catch. Overriding directly here in case that scan still doesn't fully resolve it against this bill's specific phrasing. Source: Governor of California press release (gov.ca.gov, Sept 2024); Fox 11 LA and KTLA coverage of the July 2026 compliance deadline.

states.Details: Local boards of education, district charter schools, institute charter schools, and School for the Deaf and the Blind must adopt a policy on students’ possession and use of communication devices during the school day, with specified exceptions. The department of education must make available a collection of resources and research that may assist in the development of policies.
states.VerificationNote: HB25-1135 (compliance deadline July 1, 2026) requires every local board of education and charter school to adopt, implement, and post a communication-device policy - but the bill text does not mandate a specific storage method; that's left to each district (the Colorado Department of Education publishes resources to help districts write their own policy, it doesn't prescribe pouches or lockers itself). Not a hard physical-storage mandate, so software solutions aren't precluded. Same likely root cause as California: actual bill/summary text probably lists physical storage as an example a district could choose, which the keyword classifier previously misread as a requirement. Source: Colorado Department of Education (ed.cde.state.co.us/communication-devices-in-schools); The Prowers Journal coverage of district implementation, June 2026.

states.Details: No statewide legislation found in current sources.

School districts and charter schools must adopt a policy that limits students’ cellphone use during instructional time, with specified exceptions. The department of education must provide model language that may be used to support the development of policies. Local education agencies may apply for funding under the School Cell Phone Pilot Program to provide technology solutions for students in grades 6-12 that reduce cell phone distractions during learning hours.

District school boards must adopt student code of conduct rules prohibiting elementary and middle school students’ use of a wireless communications device during the school day, and high school students’ use during instructional time, with specified exceptions. The department of education must provide a report that includes a model policy.
states.VerificationNote: HB 1105 (effective 2025-26 school year) bans phone use K-8 bell-to-bell and during HS instructional time, but doesn't mandate a storage method - Lee County requires phones zipped in backpacks (no locked container), while Escambia County evaluated and rejected Yondr pouches as cost-prohibitive. Source: NorthEscambia.com, WINK News coverage, 2025-2026.

states.Details: Local school systems and public schools must adopt a policy prohibiting bell-to-bell access to personal electronic devices by students in grades K-12, with specified exceptions. The department of education must provide guidance and technical support.
states.VerificationNote: HB 340 (K-8, effective July 2026) explicitly requires devices be "powered off and stored in lockers, locked pouches, or designated areas" - not just prohibited from use, an actual physical-storage method requirement. The Georgia Department of Education has also confirmed lockable phone storage solutions are specifically eligible for state safety grant funding, reinforcing that the state expects physical storage rather than leaving the method open. HB 1009 extends the same framework to high schools starting 2027-28. This is materially more storage-specific than the Local-discretion states above (e.g. Texas, Ohio, Michigan) and is close enough to New York/Louisiana's fact pattern to classify as Restricted rather than Ambiguous. Source: GovTech, Georgia Recorder, Atlanta News First, 13WMAZ, Capitol Beat, 2025-2026.

states.Details: No statewide legislation found in current sources.
states.VerificationNote: Hawaii's restriction came from a Board of Education policy (Policy 301-11, adopted Feb 12, 2026), not a bill - so it's invisible to NCSL and LegiScan, which only track legislation. Effective for the 2026-27 school year: cell phone use is prohibited during school hours (elementary/middle) or instructional time (high school), with exceptions for emergencies, health, and IEP needs. HIDOE has not yet published implementation guidance specifying a storage method (pouches vs. software), so compatibility genuinely is undetermined right now - worth re-checking once that guidance comes out. Source: hawaiipublicschools.org, Feb 2026.

states.Details: Local school boards and public charter schools must adopt a policy restricting students’ use of electronic communications devices so that use is as limited as possible in school buildings and on school grounds or premises during school hours and distractions in classroom settings are reduced during school hours; a policy may provide for exceptions.
No statewide legislation found in current sources.
states.VerificationNote: SB 2427, signed by Gov. Pritzker July 28, 2026, requires a bell-to-bell policy for grades K-8 (high schools have the option to restrict instructional-time use). ISBE's template policy is due Sept 1, 2026 and full implementation isn't required until the 2027-28 school year - no statewide storage method specified. This is a very recent law that may not yet be reflected in NCSL/Ballotpedia; added as an override so it isn't missed or misclassified in the meantime. Source: Fox2Now, CBS Chicago, Capitol News Illinois, July 2026.

states.Details: School corporations and charter schools must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ use of wireless communication devices during the school day, with specified exceptions. The department of education must publish model policy language and implementation guidance.

School district boards of directors must adopt a policy restricting students’ use of personal electronic devices during classroom instructional time, with specified exceptions.The department of education must develop and distribute model policies, and the state board of education may adopt rules.

School district boards of education and accredited nonpublic elementary or secondary school governing authorities must adopt policies and procedures prohibiting students from using or accessing personal electronic communication devices during the school day, with specified exceptions.
School district boards of education must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ use of personal telecommunications devices during instructional time, with specified exceptions.
Students may not possess electronic telecommunication devices throughout the instructional day, with specified exceptions.
states.VerificationNote: SB 207 (2024) is more explicit than the NCSL/Ballotpedia summary text captures: the full statute requires phones be "turned off and properly stowed away" in the student's locker, school bag, or purse for the entire instructional day - explicitly NOT in a pocket, since that counts as "on their person." That's functionally incompatible with Doorman's keep-possession, tap-to-activate model, even though it doesn't use the word "pouch." Source: KATC/Fox8/WBRZ coverage of SB 207 implementation, 2024.

states.Details: School boards must adopt a policy prohibiting student use of personal electronic devices for the duration of the school day. The department of education, in coordination with stakeholders, must make available a model policy for school boards that includes exceptions. Funds have been allocated to support costs associated with prohibiting the use of personal electronic devices during the school day.
County boards of education must develop and implement a policy to prohibit the use of electronic communication devices by students during the academic school day, with specified exceptions.
No statewide legislation found in current sources.

School district boards and public school academy boards of directors must adopt a policy prohibiting students from using a wireless communications device on school grounds during instructional time, with specified exceptions.
states.VerificationNote: HB 4141, signed by Gov. Whitmer Feb 2026, effective the 2026-27 school year, requires districts to adopt a wireless communications device policy - method is not specified in the law itself. Source: CBS Detroit, Bridge Michigan, Michigan Public, 2026.

states.Details: School districts and charter schools must adopt a policy on students’possession and use of cell phones in school. Minnesota principals’ associations must make best practices available to schools on a range of different strategies to minimize the impact of cell phones on student behavior, mental health and academic attainment.
No statewide legislation found in current sources.

School districts and charter school governing boards must adopt a policy prohibiting students from displaying or using an electronic personal communications device from the beginning of the school day until the end of the school day, with specified exceptions.
No statewide legislation found in current sources.
School boards must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ use of an electronic communication device while on school property or attending a school instructional function, with specified exceptions.
School district boards of trustees must adopt a policy limiting students’ use of an electronic communication device during instruction, with specified exceptions.

School boards and charter school boards of trustees must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ use of a personal communication device from when the first bell rings to start instructional time until the dismissal bell rings to end the academic school day, with specified exceptions.

School boards of education must adopt a policy concerning students’ use of internet-enabled devices during regular school hours, on a school bus, or during school-sanctioned events when the student is under the direct supervision of a teaching staff member or employee of the board of education. The policy must be consistent with guidelines developed by the commissioner of education.

School districts and charter schools must adopt a policy on students’ use of wireless communication devices, with specified exceptions. The public education department must issue guidelines outlining the minimum requirements for a wireless communication device policy.

School districts, charter schools and boards of cooperative educational services must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ use of internet-enabled devices during the school day anywhere on school grounds, with specified exceptions. Funds have been allocated to support the implementation of such policies.
states.VerificationNote: New York's statewide policy (announced May 2025, effective 2025-26 school year) requires phones to be stored away/off for the entire school day - schools are implementing this with physical pouches or lockers. Confirmed incompatible with a software-only approach. The NCSL/Ballotpedia summary text alone doesn't spell this out, which is why this state needed a manual override rather than relying on the keyword heuristic.

states.Details: Public school governing bodies must adopt a policy prohibiting students from using, displaying, or having a wireless communication device turned on during instructional time, with specified exceptions.
states.VerificationNote: HB 959 (Session Law 2025-38) required districts to set a policy by Jan 1, 2026 prohibiting device use/display during instructional time - the law's only requirement is the prohibition itself; storage method (backpacks, lockers, pouches, or none) is explicitly left to each district. Source: Wake Forest Law Review, Axios Raleigh, ABC11, 2025-2026.

states.Details: School districts and applicable governing bodies must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ access to a personal electronic communication device during instructional time, with specified exceptions.
School district boards of education must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ cellular telephone use during the instructional day, with specified exceptions.
states.VerificationNote: Ohio law required every district to adopt a policy prohibiting phone use for the entire school day by Jan 1, 2026, but storage method is left to districts - most use lockers or backpacks, some use pouches, and at least one district (Garfield Heights) is moving away from Yondr toward cheaper alternatives. Not a statewide physical-storage mandate. Source: Ohio Dept. of Education (education.ohio.gov), Ohio Capital Journal, 2026.

states.Details: School district boards of education must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ use of cell phones and personal electronic devices while on the campus of a public school district from bell to bell; a policy may provide for exceptions. School districts may apply for grants to purchase devices or equipment for storing cell phones during the school day.
No statewide legislation found in current sources.
Local education agencies may apply for state allocated funding for school mental health and safety and security programs, including the purchase of cell phone lockable bags.
Public schools must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ physical access to a personal electronic device as defined by the department of education, with specified exceptions.

School districts must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ access to personal electronic communication devices during the school day, as prescribed by the state board of education, as a condition for receiving state aid.
No statewide legislation found in current sources.

Failed.title: Restrict the use of a cell phone by a student during the school day
Failed.lastAction: House Do Pass Amended, Failed, YEAS 28, NAYS 39
Failed.implication: Passed the Senate but failed in the House after passing committee - a real signal of how close this got, and worth watching if it's reintroduced next session. Bill text didn't specify a storage method either way.

states.Details: Local boards of education and public charter school governing bodies must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ use of a wireless communication device during instructional time, with specified exceptions.

School district boards of trustees and governing bodies of open-enrollment charter schools must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ use of a personal communication device while on school property during the school day, with specified exceptions. The state education agency must develop and publish model language.
states.VerificationNote: HB 1481 (effective 2025-26 school year) requires every district to adopt a policy prohibiting personal device use, but leaves the storage method to each district - Dallas ISD chose magnetic pouches, Ector County ISD provides no storage at all (students responsible for keeping devices out of sight), and some elementary campuses use teacher collection. Not a statewide physical-storage mandate. Source: Click2Houston, Fox 4 Dallas-Fort Worth, Texas Tribune coverage of district rollout, 2025.

states.Details: Local educational agencies must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ use of a cellphone, smart watch, or emerging technology at a school during school hours, with specified exceptions. The state board may create one or more model policies.

School boards and approved independent schools must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ use of cell phones and non-school-issued personal electronic devices at school from arrival to dismissal, with specified exceptions. The policy must be at least as stringent as the model policy developed by the secretary of education and stakeholders.

School boards must adopt a policy restricting student cell phone and smart device possession and prohibiting student cell phone and smart device use on school property from bell to bell, with specified exceptions.
states.VerificationNote: HB1961/SB738 (2025) and SB108 (effective July 1, 2026) codify a bell-to-bell policy requiring phones "off and stored away" for the full school day. This is less clearly method-open than most other 2025-26 bell-to-bell states - "stored away" leans toward physical removal from the student's access, and at least some districts (e.g. parts of Arlington Public Schools) are implementing it with pouches. Other districts appear to be using simple backpack storage rather than a locked container, so a network-level approach may or may not satisfy a given district's literal reading - worth validating directly with a target district before investing heavily here. Classified Ambiguous rather than Restricted since nothing found specifies a locked/physical container as a requirement. Source: FFXnow, K-12 Dive, Fairfax County Public Schools, Arlington Public Schools, 2025-2026.

states.Details: School district boards of directors may adopt policies and procedures that limit the possession and use of specified paging telecommunication devices and mobile devices by students. School district boards of directors are encouraged to review recommendations provided by the office of the superintendent of public instruction when considering the adoption of such policies and procedures.
County boards of education must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ access to personal electronic devices for use in a classroom setting during instructional time, with specified exceptions.
School boards must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ use of a wireless communication device during instructional time, with specified exceptions.
School district boards of trustees must adopt policies governing student possession and use of cellular telephones and smart devices in schools.

Local educational agencies must adopt a policy prohibiting students’ possession of a personal wireless communication device on school premises at any time during the full school day; a policy may include exceptions. The state superintendent of education must develop and share a model policy.

targetStatesMeta.note: All five factors are fully automatic and refresh nightly - Feasibility and TAM from the classification/enrollment data above, Timing from a best-effort bill-text date scan, Go-to-Market Concentration from NCES high-school-size data (Doorman sells school by school per the investment memo, not district by district), and Legislative Direction from reading each state's most-advanced pending bill through the same physical/software keyword scan used on enacted law.
